newsitem.title: USA: Biogen drug gets nod from European agency.
newsitem.headline: Biogen drug gets nod from European agency.

text.p: Biogen Inc. cleared a hurdle to marketing its drug for multiple sclerosis in Europe when an influential agency issued a positive opinion of the medicine.

The interferon beta-1a drug, which will be marketed under the brand name Avonex, received a positive opinion from the Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products, the Cambridge, Mass.-based biotechnology company said.
The drug is now before the European Commission for final review. Approval, if granted, would allow Biogen to market the drug in all 15 member states of the European Union.
"The likelihood of it not getting approved now is extremely low," said David Molowa, an analyst with Bear, Stearns & Co Inc. "I would expect formal approval in March or April," he said.
As many as 350,000 Europeans suffer from the disease, which leads to degeneration of the sheath around nerves in the brain and spinal cord.

MS is more common among women and it usually first strikes between ages of 20 and 40. About 60 percent of MS patients suffer from flareups of the disease interrupted by months or years of remission, Biogen said.
Biogen's drug is meant to treat relapses.
If approved, Avonex will compete head-to-head in Europe with Betaferon, manufactured by Germany's Schering AG.

In the United States, Schering's drug, licensed for sale by Chiron Corp. of Emeryville, Calif., under the name Betaseron, has been on the market for more than three years. But Avonex, on the market just six months, has equalled Betaseron's market share in the United States, Molowa said.
"I would expect (Biogen) to become the market leader in approved countries fairly rapidly," he said. "I believe it represents a major opportunity for the company."
In the United States, labels on Betaseron and Avonex both claim the drugs reduce flareups of MS, but only the Avonex labels also claim the drug slows the disease's progression.
Molowa also said side effects of Avonex have proven milder and required doses were lower.
Biogen said it sold more than $27 million worth of the drug in the United States during the third quarter. About 250,000 to 300,000 people suffer from MS in the United States.

Israel's Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. took a step toward launching its own MS drug, Copaxone, in the United States in September when it won approval from a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel.
Molowa estimated total sales of MS drugs in Europe could reach $250 million a year and Betaferon currently has about $50 million of that.

Biogen has arranged for Swedish pharmaceutical giant AB Astra to distribute and market Avonex in the Nordic countries, while Madison, N.J.-based Schering-Plough Corp. has rights to distribute the drug in Spain. Other companies will distribute Avonex in Italy, Australia and New Zealand.
Biogen will sell the drug itself in some European markets, including France, Germany, Britain and the Benelux countries.
